title: Robinson Proof Of Fictitious Play Convergence
proof_html:
MFoGT Exercise 2.8.12 describes Robinson's proof of fictitious play convergence using admissible sequences. For an $m\times n$ matrix $A$, define for $\alpha\in\mathbb R^n$ and $\beta\in\mathbb R^m$ $$ J(\alpha)=\{j:\alpha_j=\min_k\alpha_k\}, \qquad I(\beta)=\{i:\beta_i=\max_k\beta_k\}. $$ An admissible sequence $(\alpha(t),\beta(t))$ starts with $$ \min_j\alpha_j(0)=\max_i\beta_i(0), $$ and evolves by choosing $i\in I(\beta(t))$ and $j\in J(\alpha(t))$ such that $$ \alpha(t+1)=\alpha(t)+e_iA,\qquad \beta(t+1)=\beta(t)+Ae_j. $$ This is a cumulative-payoff encoding of fictitious play.

The central quantity is $$ \mu(t)=\max_i\beta_i(t)-\min_j\alpha_j(t). $$ The proof is by induction on the matrix size. The key estimates are:

  • if all columns are useful on an interval, then the spread of the coordinates of $\alpha$ at the end of the interval is controlled by the interval length and $\|A\|$;
  • if all rows and columns are useful on an interval, then $\mu$ is controlled on that interval;
  • if a row or column is not useful, the induction hypothesis applies to the corresponding strict submatrix.

These estimates imply that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $s$ such that $\mu(t)\le\varepsilon t$ for all $t\ge s$ and all admissible sequences. From this one obtains existence of a value for $A$, and every accumulation point of the empirical mixed strategies generated by fictitious play is optimal.

References

  • [MFoGT, Section 2.8, Exercise 12] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory, references/MathFoundationsGameTheory.pdf. Robinson's admissible-sequence proof of fictitious play convergence and minimax.
